D008_m001.question:
I’ve been a performer for nearly twenty years, and my husband keeps saying I’m not myself. For about a month last fall, I was running on pure fire—rehearsing three different cabaret sets at once, rewriting songs, calling agents at 3 a.m., convinced I was going to launch this revolutionary new show that would change theater. I barely slept—like, two hours a night, but I didn’t feel tired. My mind wouldn’t shut up, ideas crashing into each other, and if someone interrupted me or questioned anything, I’d snap. I’d feel sky-high one minute, furious the next. Focusing? Impossible. I’d start rewriting lyrics, then redesign costumes, then book studio time—none of it finished.

Then it crashed. For the last two months, I can’t get out of bed. I canceled auditions—something I’ve never done. I’m exhausted all the time, even after sleeping twelve hours. I keep thinking about that offhand comment I made to a younger actress last year—was it hurtful? Did I ruin her day? I replay every awkward moment, every flubbed line, like I’m being punished for existing. I love my work, my husband… but right now, it all feels like too much.
D008_m001.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008_m002.question:
I’ve been through some real ups and downs lately—more than I can remember having in years. About three months ago, I suddenly felt like I’d been given a new lease on life. I was redoing the entire house—painting, organizing closets, calling old friends out of the blue, even started writing songs out of nowhere! I barely slept—maybe three hours a night—but I didn’t feel tired at all. My mind raced, one idea after another; I couldn’t finish anything because something else would pop into my head. I snapped at my daughter when she tried to intervene—honestly, I didn’t know why I was so angry one minute and then laughing the next.

But that high didn’t last. After about a month, I crashed. Everything felt heavy—even getting out of bed took effort. I stopped answering calls. I used to love my garden, but now it’s just weeds. I don’t feel joy in anything—not my grandkids’ visits, not even my favorite tea. I’ve started thinking I’m just a burden now, that everyone would be better off if I weren’t around. The house is messier than it’s ever been. I hate what I’ve become.
D008_m002.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008_m003.question:
I’ve been working in the ER for about four years now, and up until a few months ago, I could handle the chaos just fine. But things started shifting last winter. I’d wake up in the middle of the night with my mind racing—like ten thoughts crashing into each other at once. I’d get these bursts of energy where I’d clean my entire apartment at 3 a.m., start painting one wall, then suddenly decide to reorganize my whole kitchen, only to leave everything halfway done. Sleep felt… unnecessary, like I was finally catching up on life.

My mood flipped constantly—laughing one minute about something totally random, then snapping at my coworker over a misplaced chart. I thought I was just being productive, but then it all crashed. For two months straight, I couldn’t get out of bed. Even showering took everything I had. I stopped going to spin class, stopped texting my friends. I kept thinking I was failing at everything—that I wasn’t a good nurse anymore, that people would be better off without me. Now I’m back in that restless phase again, but I can tell it’s not right. I don’t feel like myself. I’m scared I’m losing control.
D008_m003.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008_m004.question:

About three months ago, I hit this strange patch. First, I went for nearly a month without really sleeping—like, a few hours a night, tops, but I didn’t feel tired. I was wired. I cleaned the whole building twice in one night, started fixing things—light fixtures, leaky faucets—stuff that wasn’t even my job. My thoughts were racing—kept jumping to new ideas, like I should start a cleaning business, or buy a truck, or build a shed for my wife. I couldn’t focus on one thing long enough to finish it, just bouncing around. I felt unstoppable, like I didn’t need rest.

Then it crashed. For the past two months, I can barely get out of bed. I drag myself to work, but just wiping a counter feels like lifting bricks. My wife says I did well fixing the sink, but it doesn’t feel like anything. I keep thinking about small things I messed up—leaving a light on, being late once—and I feel like I’ve failed her, like I don’t deserve forgiveness. I know it sounds silly, but it sits heavy on me.
D008_m004.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008_m006.question:
